findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the cleanup callback
findings.body: After callers invoke the returned disposer, the handler remains registered on any still-active socket. Repeated attach/dispose cycles therefore retain closures and accumulate listeners, causing stale or duplicate message processing and unbounded memory and per-message work.

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned cleanup
findings.body:
When a caller invokes the returned disposer while the socket remains active, the `"message"` handler stays registered and continues receiving messages after teardown. Repeated attach/dispose cycles also accumulate duplicate handlers and retained state.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned cleanup function
findings.body:
Any caller invoking the returned disposer expects the registered `"message"` handler to be detached. The no-op leaves it active, causing messages after teardown, duplicate handling after reattachment, and retained references.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned cleanup function
findings.body:
After cleanup is invoked, any attacker-controlled `"message"` emitted by a still-open or reused socket continues reaching the handler. This defeats teardown as a trust-boundary revocation and can trigger stale privileged behavior or accumulate duplicate handlers for denial of service.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the cleanup callback
findings.body:
On a long-lived socket, repeatedly calling `attach()` and then its returned cleanup function leaves every `"message"` listener registered. The socket retains handler closures indefinitely, and each message invokes all stale handlers, causing unbounded memory and per-message CPU growth.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
